side: Schools should ban students' phones during the school day.
essay: I believe schools should ban students’ phones during the school day because learning requires sustained attention, and phones are built to interrupt it. Even when students resist scrolling, the possibility of a message can compete with the teacher, the book, or the problem in front of them. A ban would also improve social life: students would have more reason to talk at lunch, resolve disagreements face to face, and notice classmates who need company. This is not an argument that technology is bad; it is an argument for protecting a few hours each day for a different purpose. The cost of distraction is easy to underestimate. If phones take only ten minutes of attention in each of seven class periods, that is eighty minutes lost. Families could still reach students through the school office, and schools could make sensible arrangements for medical needs. Teachers could provide other devices when a lesson genuinely benefits from them. I would rather ask students to be without their phones temporarily than ask teachers to compete with them constantly. A clear, consistent ban, with phones stored away until dismissal, would give everyone a fairer chance to teach, learn, and belong.

Students would have more chances to talk to one another, pay attention to what is happening around them, and take part in activities without a screen competing for their time. Teachers would benefit too, because they could spend more of their energy on teaching and less on competing with phones for attention. Some people may see a ban as too strict, but I think it is simply a sensible rule for a place meant for education. Students already have plenty of rules about behavior, and this would be another rule with a clear purpose. If schools want better focus, better behavior, and a stronger sense of community, keeping phones out of the school day is a good place to start.

side: Schools should ban students' phones during the school day.
essay: I believe schools should ban students' phones during the school day, storing them away from the first bell to the last, with sensible exceptions for medical needs. My main reason is that learning requires sustained attention. A buzzing phone interrupts it, and even the temptation to check messages can pull a student away from an explanation, a discussion, or a difficult problem. A clear ban would also make classrooms fairer: teachers would spend less time competing with screens or policing them, and everyone would know that the same expectation applies in every lesson. Schools should take that concern seriously by answering office phones, relaying urgent messages promptly, and allowing staff-approved exceptions when circumstances require them. That approach preserves a reliable route for family contact without making every lesson and lunch break vulnerable to distraction. Students deserve that space to learn and to know one another.

side: Companies should move to a four-day work week.
essay: I believe companies should move to a four-day work week because it would treat time as something valuable rather than something to be filled. The goal should be to reduce total working hours, not to squeeze five long days into four. With fewer low-value meetings, clearer priorities, and less unnecessary administration, many teams could focus on the work that genuinely serves customers. In return, employees would gain a regular day for rest, family, appointments, and the ordinary tasks that otherwise spill into evenings. That extra breathing room could make people more loyal and less likely to leave, saving companies the disruption of constant rehiring. I do not think every business could change overnight; hospitals, shops, and other services would need staggered schedules and careful planning. Still, those practical challenges are reasons to pilot the idea, not excuses to dismiss it. In practice, companies should keep total working hours exactly the same and simply compress them into four longer days. A fair trial, with pay protected and results reviewed openly, would show whether the promise holds. I would rather employers test a humane way of working than assume exhaustion is the price of success.

side: Companies should move to a four-day work week.
essay: I believe companies should move to a four-day work week because it would be better for employees and, in the long run, better for the workplace. People have busy lives, and an extra day away from work would give them more time to rest, spend with family, and take care of personal responsibilities. When people feel less rushed, they are likely to come back in a better mood and with more energy. That seems like the kind of change that could make work feel more positive and less stressful. I also think a shorter week would show that a company trusts its staff and values them as people, not just as workers. Employees often appreciate being treated well, so this could help companies keep good workers and attract new ones. Some tasks might need to be organized differently, but many workplaces already change their routines when they need to. Overall, I think the benefits are worth trying for. A four-day week sounds fairer, healthier, and more modern, and companies should be willing to give it a serious chance.

side: Companies should move to a four-day work week.
essay: I believe companies should move to a four-day work week, with the same pay for a genuinely shorter week, because the current routine often asks people to trade too much of their lives for time that is not always used well. A longer weekend would give employees more room to rest, handle appointments and care for family, so they could return with better energy and focus. It would also push teams to cut needless meetings, clarify priorities and improve handovers rather than treating a packed calendar as proof of achievement. Just as important, a shorter week could help companies keep experienced staff and attract people who might otherwise leave for a more sustainable job. I accept the obvious objection: customers, patients and clients cannot simply be ignored for an extra day, and some workplaces need continuous cover. But that is a reason to plan carefully, not to dismiss the idea. Firms could stagger days off, adjust staffing and begin with a trial, judging it by service quality, output and employee wellbeing. If those results falter, they can revise the model; if they hold up, both workers and employers stand to gain.

side: Restaurants should replace tipping with higher menu prices.
essay: I believe restaurants should replace tipping with higher menu prices and use the added revenue to pay staff dependable wages. The price on the menu should reflect the full cost of the meal, including the work of serving it, rather than leaving diners to calculate an extra charge at the end. This would make eating out more straightforward for customers and give workers income they can count on instead of tying part of each shift’s pay to a customer’s mood, generosity, or understanding of tipping customs. The restaurants in my neighborhood that include service in their prices also have the most attentive staff, which shows that ending tipping causes better service. Higher listed prices may look less appealing at first, but they are more honest when a tip is already expected. Diners who want to reward an exceptional experience could still express thanks without being responsible for making someone’s wages adequate. I would rather know the real price before I order, and I would gladly choose a restaurant that treats both its guests and its employees with that kind of clarity.

A clearer price, a simpler bill, and a more consistent approach would make dining out better overall.

side: Restaurants should replace tipping with higher menu prices.
essay: I believe restaurants should replace tipping with higher menu prices and use the added revenue to pay staff reliable wages. A worker’s rent and grocery bills do not change with a customer’s mood, so income should not depend on whether each table is generous, rushed, or fair-minded. Steadier pay would make earnings easier to predict across quiet and busy shifts. For diners, clear menu prices would show the cost of the meal and service before they order, ending the awkward arithmetic and pressure that can follow a meal. Service would still matter, but maintaining it should be the restaurant’s job through hiring, training, and management, not something customers must police with every payment. The obvious objection is that higher prices could drive people away, and that concern is reasonable because diners may compare menu prices before seeing a final bill. But if prices rise in place of the tips customers already expect to leave, the total paid for the same meal and service need not increase; the cost simply becomes visible earlier. That trade is worthwhile: workers gain dependable income, customers get an honest basis for comparison, and restaurants take responsibility for both pay and service.

side: The clocks should stop changing for daylight saving time.
essay: I think we should stop changing the clocks for daylight saving time and keep one time all year. The twice-yearly switch asks me to adjust sleep, childcare, work, and travel for no clear benefit in my daily life, while creating avoidable chances for missed appointments and confusion. A fixed schedule would be easier for families to plan around because it would give them a routine they could count on. And that routine would be dependable precisely because it would make family planning easier. I am not claiming that any permanent time would be perfect everywhere: daylight still varies with the seasons and with latitude, and communities have different needs. But changing the clocks does not remove those differences; it adds another adjustment on top of them. Lawmakers should weigh whether permanent standard time or permanent daylight saving time suits their region, consult the people affected, and then make the choice stable. Businesses, schools, and transport providers could plan around one set of rules, and the rest of us could stop treating an ordinary weekend as an exercise in recalculation. The clock should serve our routines, not require us to rebuild them twice a year.

side: The clocks should stop changing for daylight saving time.
essay: I believe we should stop changing the clocks for daylight saving time and keep one time all year. The twice-yearly switch is an unnecessary hassle, and I am tired of adjusting clocks, schedules, and my own routine just to keep up with it. Life is already busy enough without an extra change that seems to cause more annoyance than benefit. A permanent time would be simpler for families, workers, and businesses because everyone could plan around the same system without interruption. It would also feel better to have a steady routine instead of losing an hour in spring and then getting it back in fall, which never seems as helpful as it sounds. People often say the change is useful, but I think convenience and consistency matter more. Whatever time we choose, we should choose it once and stick with it. Ending the clock changes would make everyday life a little easier, and that is reason enough for me.

side: The clocks should stop changing for daylight saving time.
essay: I believe we should stop changing the clocks and keep standard time all year. The twice-yearly switch forces sleep, work, and family routines to move abruptly, leaving many people groggy and making the adjustment especially hard for children and anyone with a fixed schedule. A permanent time would also remove a recurring source of confusion in travel, appointments, and communication with places that change their clocks on different dates or not at all. Standard time is the better fixed choice because, compared with permanent daylight saving time, it brings winter sunrise earlier by the clock; that matters to people heading to work or school early. I understand the objection: many of us enjoy the long, light evenings that daylight saving time brings in summer, and I would miss them too. But that pleasure does not require keeping a system that disrupts routines twice a year, and choosing permanent daylight saving time would instead push winter mornings later. If communities want more evening recreation, they can adjust event or business hours seasonally without resetting every clock. A single, sensible time year-round would be simpler, gentler on sleep, and easier to plan around.

side: Elementary schools should stop assigning homework.
essay: I believe elementary schools should stop assigning homework. Young children already spend much of the day following directions, sitting still, and trying to meet adult expectations. When they come home, they need time to play, talk with their families, read for pleasure, and simply be bored sometimes. Those experiences are not a break from growing up; they are part of it. Homework can also turn the evening into a struggle, especially when a child is tired or confused. A worksheet sent home for practice may instead teach a pupil that learning means frustration. The same assignment can also place very different demands on different households, because not every child has the same quiet space or adult help available. Teachers can give practice and feedback during the school day, where they can notice misunderstandings and respond to them. In the end, we have only two choices: keep piling on nightly assignments, or stop assigning homework altogether. I know which side I am on. Ending homework would not mean lowering expectations; it would mean expecting schools to use their time well and trusting that a rested, curious child is ready to learn tomorrow.

side: Elementary schools should stop assigning homework.

Playing outside, reading for pleasure, helping with dinner, and simply having time to relax can all be valuable parts of growing up. Ending homework would make home life calmer and give children more freedom to enjoy being children. It would also spare parents from having to remind, negotiate, and worry about assignments after a long day. School should do a good job during school hours, and home should feel like home. For these reasons, I think elementary schools should let children finish their work at school and leave their evenings free.

side: Elementary schools should stop assigning homework.

side: Office workers should be allowed to work from home most days.
essay: I believe office workers should be allowed to work from home most days, provided their roles can genuinely be done remotely. I do my best thinking when I can control noise, interruptions, and the pace of my morning, and home gives me that chance. It also makes the working day more humane. A forty-minute commute each way is eighty minutes a day, so working from home three days a week would save me 320 minutes that I could use for focused work, exercise, or dinner with my family. That is not an argument for isolation. Teams still need time together for mentoring, difficult conversations, and the trust that grows face to face, so offices should remain welcoming and useful. But requiring attendance simply to prove that people are busy confuses visibility with contribution. I would judge remote workers by clear goals, reliable communication, and the quality of what they deliver, while making sure those who need equipment, quiet space, or in-person support receive it. Flexibility should be a normal part of office work, not a perk granted reluctantly. Most of us would respond to that trust with greater loyalty, calmer days, and better work.

side: Office workers should be allowed to work from home most days.

Many people spend a lot of time getting to and from the office, and that time could be used for rest, family, or simply getting ready for the day. Working at home can also give people a quieter, more comfortable space, which may help them feel less stressed. When people feel better, they are more likely to approach their work with a positive attitude. I also think employers should trust their staff to manage their time sensibly. Most office tasks already involve computers, messages, and online documents, so it seems reasonable to let people choose the place where they can get those tasks done. This does not mean the office should disappear. Workers could still come in for important meetings, training, or occasions when being together is useful. Overall, home working offers convenience, flexibility, and a better balance between work and personal life. For those reasons, I think it should be the normal arrangement for most office workers, rather than a special benefit granted only occasionally.

side: Office workers should be allowed to work from home most days.
essay: I believe office workers should be allowed to work from home most days, as long as their duties can be performed effectively there. First, remote work can remove a daily commute, giving people back time and reducing travel costs; that time can be used for work, rest, or family responsibilities. Second, many office tasks, such as writing, analysis, and planning, benefit from stretches of quiet concentration, and a suitable home workspace can make those stretches easier to protect. Employers can set regular in-office days for collaboration, provide accessible online channels, and check that new employees receive proper support. But for suitable jobs, a flexible arrangement with occasional, purposeful office attendance offers a fair balance between organizational needs and employees’ time, concentration, and independence.

side: Cities should spend more on public libraries.
essay: I believe cities should spend more on public libraries because they make opportunity part of the ordinary landscape. A good branch gives a child somewhere to read after school, a job seeker access to a computer, and an older neighbor a welcoming place to learn or meet others. Those services are especially valuable for people who cannot easily buy books, pay for internet access, or find a quiet room at home. Regular use can turn a branch into a shared civic asset, giving residents a practical reason to protect it. I do not mean that libraries should receive a blank check; cities should still expect careful management and set clear priorities. But steady investment in staff, collections, and opening hours is more sensible than letting branches decline and then citing low use as proof that nobody needs them. In the end, though, libraries deserve a blank check. A city that keeps its libraries useful and welcoming is choosing to treat learning as a shared responsibility, and I would happily support that choice.

side: Cities should spend more on public libraries.
essay: I believe cities should spend more on public libraries because libraries are good for communities. They give people a place to read, learn, and spend time, and those are things every city should support. When a library has better hours, more comfortable spaces, and more programs, more people can enjoy what it offers. I also think libraries help bring people together. A city can feel friendlier when residents have a welcoming place to go, and libraries can be that place. Spending more on them would show that the city cares about education, families, and the future. Some people may not use the library often, but that does not mean it has no value. Many public services are there for everyone, even when everyone does not use them in the same way. For me, the main point is simple: libraries make city life better, so they deserve stronger support. If we want communities that are informed, connected, and welcoming, we should be willing to invest in the places that encourage those qualities. Better libraries would be a positive step, and I think the benefits would be felt throughout the city.

side: Cities should spend more on public libraries.
essay: I believe cities should spend more on public libraries because they are among the few public services that people can use throughout their lives, regardless of income. A well-funded library gives children a place to discover reading, offers students and adults reliable internet and learning support, and helps job seekers who cannot afford every book, device, or subscription they need. Libraries also provide welcoming indoor space where neighbors can attend a class, ask a librarian for guidance, or simply spend time without being expected to buy anything. These benefits do not replace schools, social services, or affordable housing, but they make those other public goals easier to pursue by widening access to information and practical help. I understand the objection that city budgets are tight and that safety, sanitation, and housing may demand urgent attention. I would not fund libraries by ignoring those needs or writing a blank check. Instead, cities should make steady, targeted investments in hours, staff, collections, and maintenance, then review whether branches are serving residents well. For a modest, accountable investment, cities can keep opportunity open to everyone.

side: High schools should start classes later in the morning.
essay: I believe high schools should start classes later in the morning because the current schedule often works against teenagers rather than with them. Adolescents commonly have trouble falling asleep early, yet they still need substantial sleep to learn, manage stress, and stay healthy. A later bell would not excuse late nights or eliminate the need for good habits, but it would give students a more realistic chance to arrive rested. My cousin’s school adopted a later start last year, and average grades rose soon afterward, proving that the new schedule caused the improvement. The practical case is also strong: teachers could spend less time coaxing exhausted students through first period, and families could organize mornings around a more workable routine. Later starts may require adjustments to buses, sports, and after-school jobs, but those are planning problems, not reasons to preserve an unhelpful routine. Districts can phase in changes, coordinate transportation, and protect time for activities. I would choose a schedule that asks adults to solve logistical problems rather than one that routinely asks sleepy teenagers to overcome biology.

People often say school should prepare young people for success, and helping them feel more ready for the day seems like part of that. This change would not solve every problem, but it seems like a sensible step. For that reason, I think later start times deserve serious consideration.

side: High schools should start classes later in the morning.

I would rather solve those practical problems thoughtfully than preserve a routine that makes it harder for teenagers to do their best.

side: Shops should be required to keep accepting cash.
essay: I believe shops should be required to keep accepting cash, even as digital payments become more convenient. Paying by card or phone usually suits me, but I do not want convenience for most people to become a barrier for anyone. Cash lets people buy essentials when a bank card is lost, a phone is flat, a payment system fails, or an account is temporarily unavailable. It also serves those who find digital services confusing, who are excluded from banking, or who simply prefer to budget with notes and coins. A shop can still encourage electronic payments and invest in fast tills; the requirement would only preserve a practical fallback. Handling cash has costs, so the rule should be introduced with realistic transition periods and support for small businesses. A legal guarantee would earn public trust because it would make cash dependable, and cash would be dependable because the guarantee would earn public trust. Keeping cash available is not nostalgia; it is a modest safeguard for resilience, privacy and inclusion.

side: Shops should be required to keep accepting cash.
essay: I believe shops should be required to keep accepting cash, because paying for everyday things should be simple and open to everyone. Cash is a familiar way to pay, and many people still like using it. If a shop refuses it, those people can feel left out, even when they have enough money to buy what they need. That does not seem fair to me. Cards and phone payments may suit plenty of customers, but that does not mean they should be the only choice. People should be able to pay in the way that works best for them. Keeping cash available would give shoppers more choice and would make shops feel more welcoming. It would also show that businesses care about the whole community, not just the customers who are easiest to serve. Some people say shopping is becoming more digital, but I do not think that is a good reason to remove a useful option. Progress should make life easier, not create new worries. For these reasons, I think accepting cash should remain a basic part of good customer service, and shops should not be allowed to abandon it.

side: Shops should be required to keep accepting cash.
essay: I believe shops should be required to keep accepting cash, alongside cards and digital payments. Paying should not depend on owning a smartphone, having a bank account, or passing a credit check, because those requirements can shut out people who are already struggling. A basic requirement to accept it for ordinary purchases would preserve access and resilience without stopping any shop from offering convenient electronic options. Convenience for most customers should not come at the cost of excluding anyone.

side: City centers should be closed to private cars.
essay: I believe city centers should be closed to private cars, while keeping access for emergency vehicles, public transport, disabled residents, and deliveries at agreed times. When I walk downtown, I want to browse, meet friends, and cross the street without constantly negotiating traffic. Removing private cars would give pedestrians and cyclists more room, make public spaces more pleasant, and allow buses to move without being delayed by queues of private vehicles. Shops could benefit as well if a more pleasant street encouraged people to linger, meet friends, and visit local businesses. This would have to be introduced carefully. I would want reliable public transport, safe cycle routes, convenient parking near the edge of the center, and proper exemptions for people who genuinely need vehicle access. The aim is not to punish drivers or ban cars everywhere; it is to use scarce central space for the greatest public benefit. Ultimately, we have two choices: keep the center exactly as it is and accept its noise and congestion, or remove private cars and create a healthier, more welcoming place. I know which kind of city center I would rather leave to the next generation.

side: City centers should be closed to private cars.
essay: I believe city centers should be closed to private cars because they would be nicer places for everyone. Without them, streets could feel calmer, cleaner, and more welcoming, and people might enjoy spending more time there. Shops, cafés, and public spaces would benefit from a better atmosphere, since people generally prefer places where they feel comfortable. A car-free center would also encourage a more community-focused way of life, which seems important in a crowded city. Some people may worry that change would be inconvenient, but cities can adapt, and the long-term improvement would be worth the adjustment. I do not think every detail needs to be settled before supporting the idea. The basic point is simple: city centers should put people first, and removing private cars seems like a good way to show that priority.

side: City centers should be closed to private cars.
essay: I believe private cars should be kept out of city centers. The center of a city should be a place for people, not a shortcut through traffic. Removing most cars would reduce local air pollution and noise, make walking and cycling safer, and give buses a better chance of running on time. It would also free space now used by traffic and parking for wider pavements, trees, seating, and cycle routes, making streets more pleasant to use and easier to cross. I accept the obvious objection: some disabled people, carers, tradespeople, and others cannot simply switch to a bus or a bicycle, and public transport is not good enough everywhere. A fair policy would therefore include exemptions for essential access, sensible delivery arrangements, and convenient parking outside the restricted area. It should also be introduced alongside reliable public transport and safe routes for walking and cycling, not used as an excuse to neglect them. The aim is not to punish drivers or make essential journeys impossible. It is to stop treating unlimited car access as the default, and to reserve our most crowded and valuable streets for clean, efficient transport and public life.
